rounds.t: Eye anatomy, conjunctivitis, lens disorders, and refractive errors

q.s: Which layer of the eye contains the iris, ciliary body and choroid?
The anterior segment of the eye consists of:
A college student has bilateral red, watery eyes, sparse mucous discharge and a tender swollen preauricular lymph node after a cold. What is the most common cause?
e: Correct. Viral conjunctivitis is the most common type and self-resolving.

q.s: A patient with seasonal hay fever has intensely itchy, red eyes in both sides. Diagnosis?
A newborn develops eyelid swelling and purulent discharge 3 days after vaginal birth. What is the treatment?
A newborn develops conjunctivitis 10 days after vaginal delivery. Which organism and treatment are most likely?
o: Chlamydia trachomatis serotypes D–K; erythromycin or azithromycin

q.s: A 46-year-old has to hold books farther away to read. What is the likely mechanism?
A 72-year-old smoker has gradually worsening, painless blurry vision with glare from headlights at night. The red reflex is diminished. Diagnosis?
Which is a congenital risk factor for cataract?
e: Correct. Also galactokinase deficiency, TORCH (rubella), trisomies.

q.s: What is the treatment for cataract?
o: Surgical replacement with an artificial lens

q.s: A tall man with long fingers has upward dislocation of both lenses. Which condition is most likely?
e: Correct. Ectopia lentis; homocystinuria usually dislocates downward.

q.s: Which genetic conditions are associated with lens dislocation?
A child cannot see the board at school but reads well up close. The eye is too long for its refractive power. Which lens corrects this?
In hyperopia, light focuses:
e: Correct. Eye too short; correct with a convex lens.

q.s: Astigmatism is corrected with which lens?
e: Correct. Irregular curvature of cornea or lens.

q.s: What is the most common refractive error?
e: Wrong. Not a refractive error of eye length.

q.s: Bacterial conjunctivitis typically presents with:
Which acquired risk factor causes cataracts?
e: Correct. Also age, smoking, alcohol, sunlight, diabetes, trauma.

q.s: Neonatal gonococcal conjunctivitis is prevented with:
The lens is suspended from the ciliary body by:
e: Correct. Ciliary muscle changes lens shape.

q.s: Aqueous humor is produced by:
o: Nonpigmented epithelium of the ciliary body

q.s: Most aqueous humor drains through which route?
o: Trabecular meshwork to the canal of Schlemm

q.s: Latanoprost lowers intraocular pressure by:
o: Contracting the ciliary muscle via M3

q.s: Which drug lowers IOP by decreasing aqueous humor production?
e: Correct. β-blocker; also brimonidine and acetazolamide.

q.s: Pilocarpine increases trabecular outflow by acting on which receptor?
e: Correct. Contracts ciliary muscle and pupillary sphincter.

q.s: The pupillary dilator muscle is innervated through which receptor?
Glaucoma causes vision loss in which pattern?
Funduscopy in glaucoma shows:
o: Optic disc cupping from thinning of the outer rim

q.s: A 65-year-old Black man with a family history of glaucoma has increased cup-to-disc ratio found at a routine visit. He has no symptoms. Which mechanism is responsible?
o: Increased resistance to drainage through the trabecular meshwork

q.s: First-line treatment of open-angle glaucoma includes:

In angle-closure glaucoma, what causes the iris to block drainage?
o: Pupillary block increases posterior chamber pressure, pushing the peripheral iris against the cornea

q.s: Which secondary cause of glaucoma is identified?
Which drug combination is used for acute angle-closure glaucoma?
o: β-blocker, α2-agonist, pilocarpine, acetazolamide and mannitol

q.s: Which is the most common type of glaucoma in the US?
The mnemonic for acute angle-closure glaucoma is:
o: Hurts in a hurry with halos, a headache and a "half-dilated" pupil

q.s: Acetazolamide lowers IOP by inhibiting:
Brimonidine lowers IOP by:
o: Activating α2 receptors to decrease aqueous production

q.s: Why is acute angle-closure glaucoma an emergency?
o: Rapidly rising IOP can cause permanent blindness
It spreads to the other eye immediately

q.s: Which risk factor is associated with open-angle glaucoma?
o: Diabetes mellitus, age, family history and Black race

q.s: An 80-year-old has gradual loss of central vision. Funduscopy shows yellow subretinal deposits. Diagnosis?
A 78-year-old notices straight lines looking wavy, followed by rapid loss of central vision. What causes this?
e: Correct. Wet AMD; metamorphopsia is an early symptom.

q.s: Vision loss in nonproliferative diabetic retinopathy is mainly due to:
Which finding defines proliferative diabetic retinopathy?
Complications of proliferative diabetic retinopathy include:
o: Vitreous hemorrhage and tractional retinal detachment

q.s: A man with BP 220/130 mm Hg has headache and blurred vision. Funduscopy shows AV nicking, flame hemorrhages, a macular star and blurred disc margins. What does the disc finding indicate?
o: Hypertensive emergency requiring immediate BP lowering

q.s: A 70-year-old with carotid disease has sudden painless loss of vision in one eye. Funduscopy shows a pale, cloudy retina with a cherry-red spot at the fovea. Diagnosis?
Small yellow refractile deposits in retinal arterioles seen in retinal artery occlusion are:
A hypertensive 68-year-old has sudden painless blurred vision. Funduscopy shows widespread retinal hemorrhages and engorged veins. Which mechanism caused it?
o: Embolism to the central retinal artery
Thrombosis of the central retinal vein

q.s: Branch retinal vein occlusion usually occurs at:
o: Arteriovenous crossings where a sclerotic arteriole compresses a venule

q.s: A highly myopic 60-year-old sees new floaters and flashes of light, then a dark curtain over part of his vision. What is the most common type of this disorder?
o: Rhegmatogenous retinal detachment from a retinal tear

q.s: Retinal detachment causes vision loss because:
o: Photoreceptors lose their choroidal blood supply

q.s: A 20-year-old has night blindness and loss of peripheral vision. Funduscopy shows a pale optic disc, thin vessels and bone spicule–shaped pigment. Diagnosis?
e: Correct. May be associated with abetalipoproteinemia.

q.s: In retinopathy of prematurity, the neovascularization is driven by:
o: Hypoxia of avascular retina increasing VEGF

q.s: Why does supplemental oxygen for neonatal respiratory distress increase the risk of retinopathy of prematurity?
o: Relative hyperoxia reduces VEGF and arrests normal retinal vascularization

q.s: An 18-month-old has a white pupil in photographs and a squint. What is the genetic defect in this tumor?
o: Loss of both RB1 alleles on chromosome 13

q.s: The RB protein normally:
Nonproliferative diabetic retinopathy findings include:
o: Microaneurysms, hemorrhages, cotton-wool spots and hard exudates

q.s: Papilledema results from:
o: Impaired axoplasmic flow in the optic nerve from increased ICP

q.s: Funduscopy in papilledema shows:
o: Elevated optic disc with blurred margins, usually bilateral

q.s: Important causes of leukocoria in children include:

Which systemic diseases are associated with uveitis?
o: Sarcoidosis, Behçet syndrome, juvenile idiopathic arthritis and HLA-B27 conditions

q.s: Inflammation of the iris is called:
Posterior uveitis involves:

A child with sinusitis develops fever, proptosis, painful eye movements and double vision. Diagnosis?
e: Correct. S aureus and streptococci; risk of cavernous sinus thrombosis.

q.s: Orbital cellulitis is most often secondary to:
A woman has a painful, red, tender nodule on her eyelid margin. Diagnosis?
e: Correct. Acute infection of eyelid glands.

q.s: A painless, firm eyelid nodule develops over weeks from a blocked meibomian gland. Diagnosis?
Yellowish plaques on the medial eyelids may be associated with:

rounds.t: Pupillary control, relative afferent pupillary defect, and Horner syndrome

q.s: Parasympathetic fibers for pupillary constriction originate in which nucleus?
e: Correct. Travel via CN III to the ciliary ganglion.

q.s: Postganglionic parasympathetic fibers reach the sphincter pupillae via the:
e: Correct. "Short ciliary nerves shorten the pupil diameter."

q.s: In the pupillary light reflex, CN II carries the signal to which midbrain nuclei?
e: Correct. These activate both Edinger-Westphal nuclei.

q.s: Shining light into one eye causes both pupils to constrict because:
o: CN III crosses at the chiasm
Pretectal nuclei activate both Edinger-Westphal nuclei
The sympathetic system is inhibited bilaterally
Each optic nerve reaches only one side

q.s: The first-order sympathetic neuron to the eye travels from the hypothalamus to:
Third-order sympathetic neurons to the eye travel:
o: With CN III to the ciliary ganglion
Along the internal carotid artery, through the cavernous sinus, as the long ciliary nerve

q.s: A patient with right optic neuritis is tested with the swinging flashlight. When light moves from the left eye to the right eye, both pupils dilate. This is called:
o: Relative afferent pupillary defect (Marcus Gunn pupil)

q.s: A relative afferent pupillary defect indicates a lesion of:
o: The retina or optic nerve (afferent limb)

q.s: Sympathetic fibers also innervate which structures on the face?
o: Eyelid smooth muscle and forehead/facial sweat glands

q.s: A 55-year-old smoker has right shoulder pain, a drooping right eyelid, a small right pupil and lack of sweating on the right face. Chest x-ray shows a right apical mass. Which neuron is affected?
o: Second-order neuron at the stellate ganglion
Third-order neuron in the cavernous sinus
e: Correct. Pancoast tumor causing Horner syndrome.

q.s: A young woman has sudden right neck pain after a chiropractic manipulation, followed by right ptosis and miosis without anhidrosis. Diagnosis?
o: Internal carotid artery dissection affecting third-order neurons
e: Correct. Painful; anhidrosis is usually absent.

q.s: Which lesion causes Horner syndrome via first-order neurons?
e: Correct. Also pontine hemorrhage and cord lesions above T1.

q.s: The ptosis in Horner syndrome is mild because it involves:
e: Wrong. CN III causes severe ptosis.

q.s: The triad of Horner syndrome is:
Which cord lesion can cause Horner syndrome?
o: Late-stage syringomyelia or Brown-Séquard above T1

q.s: Second-order sympathetic neurons travel near which structures, making them vulnerable?
o: The lung apex and subclavian vessels

q.s: Why is anhidrosis usually absent in carotid dissection Horner syndrome?
o: Facial sweat fibers travel with the external carotid, which is spared
Sweating is controlled by CN VII
Sweat fibers travel with CN III

q.s: Long ciliary nerves carry:
o: Parasympathetic fibers to the sphincter pupillae
Sympathetic fibers to the pupillary dilator
e: Correct. "Long ciliary nerves make the pupil diameter longer."

q.s: When light is shone in a normal eye of a patient with an optic nerve lesion on the other side:
e: Wrong. That happens when swinging to the affected eye.

After being punched in the eye, a man has double vision on upward gaze, a sunken eye and numbness of his cheek. Which bone is fractured?
e: Correct. Blowout fracture with IR entrapment and infraorbital nerve injury.

q.s: A child with an orbital trapdoor fracture has bradycardia, nausea and syncope when attempting upgaze. What does this indicate?
o: Oculocardiac reflex from muscle entrapment requiring urgent surgery

q.s: The most common type of strabismus in children is:
Amblyopia results from:
o: Maldevelopment of the visual cortex from abnormal early visual experience

q.s: A 60-year-old diabetic has sudden diplopia. His right eye is down and out with ptosis, but the pupil is normal and reactive. Mechanism?
o: Ischemia of central motor fibers with sparing of peripheral parasympathetic fibers
q.k: Cranial nerve III, IV, VI palsies

q.s: A patient has sudden severe headache with a dilated, nonreactive left pupil and left ptosis. Why is the pupil involved early?
o: Parasympathetic fibers lie on the periphery and are compressed first
Motor fibers are in the center of the nerve
e: Wrong. That explains sparing in ischemia.
q.k: Cranial nerve III, IV, VI palsies

q.s: A patient with fever, proptosis and painful eyes has a CN III palsy plus involvement of CN IV, V1, V2 and VI. Which cause is most likely?
q.k: Cranial nerve III, IV, VI palsies

q.s: A patient with a CN III palsy and contralateral hemiplegia most likely has:
q.k: Cranial nerve III, IV, VI palsies

q.s: After a head injury, a patient has vertical diplopia, difficulty walking downstairs and tilts his head to the left. Which nerve is injured?
e: Correct. Tilts to the unaffected side to compensate for lost intorsion.
Wrong. Head tilts away from the lesion.

q.k: Cranial nerve III, IV, VI palsies

e: Correct. Affected eye is displaced medially.
q.k: Cranial nerve III, IV, VI palsies

q.s: Why does diabetes affect the CN III motor fibers more than parasympathetic fibers?
o: Central motor fibers depend on diffusion from compromised vessels on the outside of the nerve
q.k: Cranial nerve III, IV, VI palsies

q.s: Uncal herniation causing a CN III palsy typically presents with:
q.k: Cranial nerve III, IV, VI palsies

rounds.t: Visual field defects, cavernous sinus, and internuclear ophthalmoplegia

q.s: A patient with macular degeneration has which visual field defect?
A lesion of the left optic nerve causes:
o: Complete loss of vision in the left eye (left anopia)

q.s: A 40-year-old woman with a pituitary macroadenoma bumps into door frames on both sides. Which visual field defect is expected?
e: Correct. Compression of the optic chiasm.

q.s: Meyer loop carries fibers from which part of the retina?

CN II, CN VII and the vertebral artery

q.s: Which CN in the cavernous sinus lies freely within the sinus next to the internal carotid artery, rather than in the lateral wall?

q.s: Cavernous sinus syndrome may result from:
o: Pituitary tumor, carotid-cavernous fistula or infection-related thrombosis

q.s: When looking left, which nucleus fires first to move both eyes?
o: Left CN VI nucleus, which signals the right CN III nucleus via the right MLF

q.s: A right INO refers to:
o: The right eye failing to adduct, from a right MLF lesion

q.s: In INO, convergence is normal because:
o: Convergence does not depend on the MLF connection

q.s: Bilateral INO in a young adult is classically due to:

Correct. The MLF is highly myelinated.

q.s: In INO, the abducting eye shows nystagmus because:
o: CN VI overfires to try to stimulate CN III
